heroLead: Thompson Springs is a near-ghost town along the old rail line north of Moab, and the mineral history under it is stranger and more layered than most Utah towns its size ever get.
intro: Thompson Springs once serviced a working rail depot and coal-loading point, then became a staging ground during the mid-century uranium and vanadium boom that swept through eastern Utah, and today it's mostly empty storefronts and a handful of year-round residents. What survives from that history, for our purposes, is a patchwork of old mineral deeds and reservations, some referencing oil and gas, some referencing uranium and vanadium specifically, occasionally on the very same tract.

We approach a Thompson Springs interest expecting some research to be required. Old Grand County deeds from the boom era were not always written with the clarity a modern title examiner would want, and sorting out what a family actually holds today often takes real work at the courthouse.

sections.heading: Uranium and vanadium legacy alongside oil and gas
paragraphs: Grand County's stretch of the Colorado Plateau, including the area around Thompson Springs, produced uranium and vanadium ore for the Cold War-era market, and some deeds from that period reserved those substances specifically rather than minerals broadly. If your family's paperwork mentions uranium or vanadium by name, that's a different asset class than oil and gas royalty, and we evaluate it separately.

Where a deed does grant minerals broadly, any oil and gas potential tied to the Paradox Basin formations in this corner of Grand County is a separate consideration we research against current activity.

sections.heading: A quiet corner of the Paradox Basin
paragraphs: Thompson Springs sits north of the more actively drilled Cane Creek trend near Moab, in a part of the basin that's seen less recent horizontal activity. That doesn't make an interest here worthless, it just means we price it more conservatively, closer to a long-dated option on future development than an interest with active nearby permitting.
We keep an eye on Grand County permitting broadly, since activity has a way of migrating along a trend over a period of years, and a quiet interest today isn't necessarily quiet indefinitely.

sections.heading: Reconstructing an old chain of title
paragraphs: Because Thompson Springs' population has shrunk so dramatically since its rail and mining days, family documentation is often incomplete, sometimes just a name mentioned in an old will or a faded tax notice. We do the work of tracing the chain through the Grand County recorder's office in Moab, and we're comfortable starting from a thin paper trail rather than requiring you to reconstruct it yourself first.

faqs.question: My old deed mentions uranium and vanadium, not oil and gas. What does that mean?
faqs.answer: It means the interest was written specifically for those substances during the mid-century mining boom. We evaluate uranium and vanadium interests on their own terms, separate from any oil and gas potential on the same land.

faqs.question: Is there any current oil and gas activity near Thompson Springs?
faqs.answer: Less than the more active Cane Creek trend closer to Moab. We price interests here more conservatively as a result, though we do track how activity migrates along the broader Paradox Basin trend over time.

faqs.question: I only have a name from an old family will, no formal deed. Can you still work with that?
faqs.answer: Yes. We research the Grand County recorder's records to reconstruct the chain of title starting from whatever partial information you have.
